After the Rain is a live-action short coming soon from Little Wild Films.

## About the film

The rain stops. The power goes out. For a few minutes, the city has to look at itself without the usual glow.

After the Rain is a live-action study in atmosphere, memory, and the things that become visible when the familiar systems go quiet.

## Working note

This film is being developed as a compact, location-led piece: a small crew, practical light, and a camera willing to wait.

Mosslight is an AI-assisted visual experiment by Little Wild Films.

## About the film

Mosslight began as a question: can a place hold a memory without turning it into a ghost story?

The project uses generative tools as a sketchbook for a forest that changes with every person who enters it.

## The experiment

Rather than asking a model for a finished image, we are using it to discover the edges of a world — then bringing those discoveries back into a more deliberate filmmaking process.

The Lantern in the Orchard is an animated short in development by Little Wild Films.

## About the film

The orchard has always known when spring is coming. This year, it forgets.

A child carrying a paper lantern walks between the trees, looking for the one blossom that still remembers the season. Along the way, the orchard begins to return small pieces of the past: a lost ribbon, a song from an empty house, the sound of rain on a roof that no longer exists.

## Director’s note

I wanted to make a film about wonder without making the world feel weightless. The visual language begins with hand-painted animation, quiet landscapes, and the warmth of a small light against a large night.

The film is interested in the spaces between adventure and stillness — the moment before a door opens, the path after everyone else has gone home, and the feeling that a place might be waiting for you.

## Credits

The film is written and directed by Little Wild Films, with visual development and worldbuilding developed in-house.

## About the film

At the edge of a familiar coast, a child discovers that blue hour is not a time of day but a thing that can be carried.

The film is a small fable about endings, attention, and the light we keep for one another.

## Director’s note

We made this as an exercise in restraint: fewer words, longer looks, and a world that changes almost imperceptibly while the character is watching.

Building a forest that feels remembered
Notes on making a forest feel like it existed before the camera arrived.
A blue-hour valley with a single warm light on a winding path.
Process notes from building the remembered forest in The Lantern in the Orchard.

The first version of the forest looked beautiful, but it felt empty.

It had the right trees, the right light, and the right atmosphere. But it did not feel like a place that had existed before the camera arrived.

## The problem with beautiful images

When an image is too perfect, there is nowhere for the viewer’s imagination to enter.

For *The Lantern in the Orchard*, we began introducing small imperfections: paths that disappeared, trees that leaned toward the light, and details that felt almost remembered rather than clearly designed.

## Leaving room for the viewer

The most important part of the forest is not what we show. It is what the frame leaves unresolved.

A distant light can be a home, a memory, or just a reflection on wet grass. The film does not need to decide immediately. It only needs to make the question feel worth carrying into the next shot.

> A world becomes believable when it has a life outside the frame.

This is the kind of quiet uncertainty we are trying to protect as the film grows.

Blue hour is a narrow door.

It does not stay open long enough for certainty, which is exactly why it felt right for this film.

## Looking for the in-between

We kept returning to photographs where the sky was not quite blue and the ground was not quite dark. The image had to feel like it was changing while we looked at it.

For the film, that became a rule: every frame should carry a little of the previous light and a little of the next darkness.

The useful prompt is often the one that fails beautifully.

For Mosslight, we are less interested in asking a machine to finish a forest than in asking it to show us a forest we would not have thought to draw.

## Keep the question alive

The job of direction is to decide what to keep, what to reject, and what new question an image creates. The tool can provide momentum, but it cannot decide what the film means.

That part still belongs to attention.

Why weather is not background in After the Rain — it is part of the edit.
A cinematic mountain landscape after a storm.
Production notes on weather, continuity, and atmosphere in After the Rain.

Weather changes the rhythm of a scene before anyone speaks.

In After the Rain, the storm is not an event we cut away from. It is the thing that makes the city briefly unfamiliar.

## Practical atmosphere

The production question is simple but difficult: how do we let the weather shape the performance without asking the weather to perform on cue?

The answer so far is patience. We are building the schedule around the sky instead of asking the sky to fit inside the schedule.
